title: The reason in things
hook: Stoics saw a reason running through all things

segments.voice: Yesterday: live by nature, Zeno's goal. Your line was in agreement. Did you get your five minutes outside? Day two hundred eighty-nine.

Cut an apple across the middle, not top to bottom, and you'll find a five-pointed star. Look at a sunflower's center and the seeds curl out in two sets of spirals, one clockwise, one counter. Your heartbeat speeds up when you climb stairs and settles when you sit. The tide comes in about twice a day, and a little later each day. None of this is random. There's an order to things, and people have been noticing it for as long as there have been people. The Stoics gave that order a name. Today: logos.
screen: `A STAR INSIDE AN APPLE.` → `SPIRALS IN A SUNFLOWER.` → `THERE'S AN ORDER.`

segments.voice: Logos is one of the busiest words in Greek. It can mean word, speech, story, account, reason, even ratio. It comes from a verb that means to say, and before that, to gather or pick out. You hear it in English every time you say logic, or biology, the account of life. About two centuries before Zeno, a philosopher named Heraclitus of Ephesus used logos for the order behind the world, and complained that it's common to all of us, yet most people live as if they had a private understanding of their own. The Stoics took the word and built on it. For them, the logos is the reason running through everything, the rational pattern that shapes a seed into a tree and keeps the stars in their tracks. They pictured it as active and alive, a kind of fiery breath moving through matter. And they gave it many names at once: nature, fate, providence, even Zeus or God. Stoics disagreed among themselves about details, and the sources are fragmentary, so it's fair to say we only see the outline. Here's why this matters for a person, not just for the cosmos. The Stoics said each of us carries a small share of that same reason. When you think clearly, you're doing on a small scale what the world does on a large one. That's why living by reason and living by nature were the same thing to them. The same Greek word appears in the Gospel of John, where Christians read it their own way; for the Stoics, the logos was the pattern itself.
screen: `LOGOS — WORD, REASON, ACCOUNT.` · `HERACLITUS: COMMON TO ALL.` · `A REASON RUNNING THROUGH EVERYTHING.` · `A SMALL SHARE IN EACH OF US.` · then, large: `THE PATTERN.`

segments.voice: Start with the nearest pattern: your breath. In, a turn at the top, out, a pause at the bottom. Nobody is running it, and it runs. Let it go on by itself and just watch the shape of it. If your mind wanders, that's a pattern too. Come back to the breath, one turn, then the next. The bell holds the time.
Logos. Greek for word, reason or account: for the Stoics, the reason running through all things, shared in each of us. Today's word.
Your line: the pattern. Notice one pattern in nature today, a leaf's veins, the light shifting, birds lining up on a wire, and stay with it a moment. Day two hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Many who practice Stoicism today treat the logos as the rational order of nature, whether they understand it religiously or not, and try to think clearly as their share in it.

fork.setup: Heraclitus says the logos is common to all. what does he complain most people do?
options: live as if they had a private understanding.
fork.reveal: Heraclitus complains that though the logos is shared, most live as if their understanding were private.
